mis.m: Writes the 7 in 3.407 as 7 tenths, or 0.7, in expanded notation.
mis.why: Students count places from the left of the whole number or skip the zero placeholder.
mis.fix: Have students label each digit's place on a place value chart before writing any term, saying the place name aloud for the zero too.

mis.m: Writes 2.36 in expanded notation as 2 + 3 + 6 or 2 + 0.3 + 0.6.
mis.why: Students list the digits instead of the value each digit represents.
mis.fix: Ask 'How much is the 6 worth?' and have students build it with place value disks before writing 0.06.

mis.m: Thinks thousandths are larger than hundredths because 'thousand' is bigger than 'hundred.'
mis.why: Whole-number place names grow to the left, so students carry that sense of size into decimal names.
mis.fix: Cut a hundredths grid square into 10 slivers so students see one thousandth is a tenth of one hundredth.

cra.c: Students build decimals such as 4.215 with place value disks on a place value mat, trading one tenth disk for ten hundredths disks to see the 10-to-1 relationship.
cra.r: Students record the number on a place value chart and write each part as an addend, using a number line zoomed from tenths to hundredths to thousandths to show where the value sits.
cra.a: Students write the decimal in expanded notation in both forms, such as 4 + 0.2 + 0.01 + 0.005 and (4 × 1) + (2 × 0.1) + (1 × 0.01) + (5 × 0.001).
cra.look: Students point to each disk or column while naming its value, and match standard form, word form and expanded notation cards.

assess: How did you decide the value of the 5 in 6.025?
Why do you need a zero in the tenths place here?
advance: How would the value change if the 5 moved one place to the left?
Write a decimal whose expanded notation has exactly three terms and a zero in the hundredths.

assess: Show me with disks how much the 3 is worth.
Which part of your expanded notation matches this column?
advance: How many thousandths are in one hundredth? Prove it with the disks.
Can you write the same number with multiplication in each term?

assess: Point to the tenths column.
Is this digit worth 4 hundredths or 4 thousandths?
advance: Put 4 hundredths disks on the mat. What decimal did you make?
Read the number aloud using the place names.
support: Give a place value chart with only ones, tenths and hundredths columns first, then add thousandths.
Color-code disks and chart columns by place so students match by color, then by name.

stems: The digit ___ is in the ___ place, so its value is ___.
In expanded notation, ___ is written as ___.
I need a zero in the ___ place because ___.
One thousandth is ___ times smaller than one hundredth.
I agree with ___ because the value of the digit is ___.
d: Represent the value of digit in decimals through the thousandths using expanded notation and numerals.

mis.m: Says 0.45 > 0.6 because 45 is greater than 6.
mis.why: Students compare the digits after the point as whole numbers instead of comparing place by place.
mis.fix: Have students write both numbers in a place value chart aligned on the decimal point and compare the tenths first.

mis.m: Says 0.125 > 0.13 because it has more digits.
mis.why: Students assume longer numbers are larger, a rule that works for whole numbers.
mis.fix: Annex zeros so both have the same number of places (0.125 and 0.130), then compare thousandths to thousandths.

mis.m: Orders a set from least to greatest correctly but writes the symbol pointing the wrong way.
mis.why: Students memorize symbol tricks without connecting the symbol to the phrase 'is greater than' or 'is less than.'
mis.fix: Have students read every statement aloud in words and check it against a number line before writing the symbol.

cra.c: Students build both decimals with base-ten blocks (flat as one whole) or place value disks and compare the amount of each piece starting from the largest place.
cra.r: Students plot both decimals on a number line partitioned into tenths, then hundredths, then thousandths, so the number to the right is greater.
cra.a: Students align the numbers on the decimal point, annex zeros when needed, compare place by place and write the statement with >, < or =.
cra.look: Students line up decimal points, annex zeros, and justify each comparison by pointing to the first place where the digits differ.

assess: Which place did you look at first, and why?
How does your number line show which decimal is greater?
advance: Find a decimal between 0.34 and 0.35.
Order four decimals where the longest one is the smallest.

assess: Why did you add a zero to 0.7?
Read your comparison aloud in words.
advance: How could 2.09 and 2.090 both be correct?
Which of these is closest to 1, and how do you know?

assess: Which number has more tenths?
Point to the number farther right on the number line.
advance: Now compare the hundredths. What do you notice?
Write the symbol and read it to me in words.
support: Provide a place value chart template with the decimal point already drawn.
Start with pairs that differ in the tenths, then move to pairs that differ in the hundredths and thousandths.

stems: ___ is greater than ___ because in the ___ place ___.
I added a zero to ___ so I could compare ___.
On the number line, ___ is to the right of ___, so ___.
From least to greatest, the order is ___ because ___.
I disagree with ___ because more digits does not mean ___.
d: Compare and order two decimals to thousandths and represent comparisons using the symbols >, <, or =.

mis.m: Rounds 3.476 to the nearest tenth as 3.48.
mis.why: Students round to the place immediately before the last digit instead of the place requested.
mis.fix: Have students underline the rounding place and circle only the digit to its right before deciding.

mis.m: Rounds 2.96 to the nearest tenth as 2.10 or 2.9 instead of 3.0.
mis.why: Students do not regroup when the rounding digit is 9 and rounds up.
mis.fix: Use a number line from 2.9 to 3.0 so students see the next tenth after 2.9 is 3.0.

mis.m: Rounds 5.349 to the nearest tenth as 5.4 by rounding the 9 first, then the 4.
mis.why: Students chain-round from the right instead of looking only at the digit next to the rounding place.
mis.fix: Place 5.349 on a number line between 5.3 and 5.4 and mark the halfway point 5.35 to show it falls below.

cra.c: Students build the decimal with place value disks and decide whether it is closer to the tenth or hundredth below or above it, using a number line drawn on tape on the floor.
cra.r: Students draw a vertical or horizontal number line, label the two benchmark decimals and the halfway point, then plot the number.
cra.a: Students identify the rounding place, look at the digit to its right, and write the rounded decimal, checking that it matches the closer benchmark.
cra.look: Students sketch number lines with both benchmarks and the halfway point labeled before writing the rounded value.

assess: Which two tenths is 6.83 between?
How did you use the halfway point?
advance: Name three decimals that round to 4.7.
What is the greatest hundredths decimal that rounds to 8.2?

assess: Show me the benchmark numbers on your number line.
Which digit told you to round up or down?
advance: Why does 1.96 round to 2.0 and not 1.10?
Round the same number to the nearest hundredth. What changed?

assess: Put your finger on the tenths place.
Is 4.32 closer to 4.3 or 4.4?
advance: Mark the halfway point between 4.3 and 4.4. What is it?
Does 4.36 land before or after that point?
support: Provide number lines with benchmarks pre-labeled so students only plot and decide.
Use money: round $3.68 to the nearest dime with coins to connect tenths to dimes.

stems: ___ is between ___ and ___.
The halfway point is ___, so ___ rounds to ___.
I looked at the digit in the ___ place because ___.
Rounding to the nearest tenth, ___ becomes ___.
I agree with ___ because on the number line ___.
d: Round decimals to tenths or hundredths.

mis.m: Computes the exact answer first, then rounds it and calls that the estimate.
mis.why: Students see estimation as an extra step rather than a tool to predict or check.
mis.fix: Ask for the estimate before any computation and record it on the board, then compare it to the exact answer later.

mis.m: Rounds 48 × 23 as 50 × 30 and claims a close estimate without noticing it is much too high.
mis.why: Students round each factor the same way without considering how rounding affects the product.
mis.fix: Have students compare two estimates (50 × 20 and 50 × 25) and discuss which is closer and why.

mis.m: For 3,215 ÷ 41 rounds to 3,000 ÷ 40 and gets stuck, or rounds to 3,200 ÷ 40 without seeing a friendlier choice.
mis.why: Students round to the nearest place automatically instead of choosing compatible numbers.
mis.fix: Model listing multiples of 40 (2,800, 3,200, 3,600) and choosing the one closest to the dividend.

cra.c: Students use base-ten blocks or play money to show a rounded amount next to an exact amount, seeing how close the two collections are.
cra.r: Students place exact values on a number line between benchmarks, and draw strip diagrams labeled with rounded or compatible numbers.
cra.a: Students write the estimate equation with rounded or compatible numbers and use it to judge whether an exact answer is reasonable.
cra.look: Students write an estimate before computing and refer back to it to check their final answer.

assess: Why did you pick those compatible numbers?
Is your estimate higher or lower than the exact answer? How do you know?
advance: When would an overestimate be safer than an underestimate in this situation?
Find an estimate that is closer, and explain what you changed.

assess: Show me where 487 sits between benchmarks on your number line.
What rounded numbers did you use?
advance: Does your exact answer make sense compared to your estimate?
Could someone round differently and still be reasonable?

assess: Is 52 closer to 50 or 60?
What is 50 + 30?
advance: Use your estimate to check: is 812 a reasonable answer?
Which strip in your diagram is the larger amount?
support: Provide a hundreds chart or number line to locate benchmarks quickly.
Start with two-number addition and subtraction estimates before multiplication and division.

stems: I rounded ___ to ___ because ___.
My estimate is ___, so the answer should be about ___.
I chose compatible numbers ___ and ___ because ___.
The exact answer is reasonable because it is close to ___.
My estimate is greater than the exact answer because ___.
d: Estimate to determine solutions to mathematical and real-world problems involving addition, subtraction, multiplication, or division.

mis.m: In 346 × 27, multiplies by the 2 in the tens place but forgets the placeholder zero, adding 2,422 + 692.
mis.why: Students treat the tens digit as 2 instead of 20.
mis.fix: Have students say '346 times 20' and write the zero before multiplying by the 2.

mis.m: Adds the regrouped digit before multiplying, such as writing 4 + 1 = 5, then 5 × 7.
mis.why: Students confuse the order of operations within the algorithm.
mis.fix: Model 'multiply, then add what you carried' with a think-aloud and a matching area model partial product.

mis.m: Leaves the regrouped digits from the ones row in place when multiplying by the tens digit, adding them in again.
mis.why: Students do not clear or separate the regrouped digits between rows.
mis.fix: Have students cross out regrouped digits after the first row, or record them in a different color for each row.

cra.c: Students build a small case such as 23 × 14 with base-ten blocks in an array to see four partial products before moving to larger numbers.
cra.r: Students draw an area model for the three-digit by two-digit product, labeling each partial product, and match each row of the standard algorithm to parts of the area model.
cra.a: Students use the standard algorithm, then check with an estimate to judge whether the product is reasonable.
cra.look: Students write the placeholder zero, connect algorithm rows to area model sections, and check products against estimates.

assess: Which part of the area model matches the second row of the algorithm?
Why does the second row start with a zero?
advance: Without computing, how would the product change if the 27 became 37?
Find the error in this worked example and explain it.

assess: Show me 346 × 7 in your area model.
What did you carry, and where did it come from?
advance: Compare your product to your estimate. Is it reasonable?
Could you break 27 differently and get the same product?

assess: What is 6 × 7?
Where do you write the 2 you carried?
advance: Now multiply 346 × 20. What happens to the place of each digit?
Add the two rows. Does the sum look like your estimate?
support: Provide graph paper so digits stay aligned in place value columns.
Give a multiplication chart to reduce fact load while practicing the algorithm steps.

stems: First I multiplied ___ by ___ to get ___.
I wrote a zero in the second row because I am multiplying by ___ tens.
This partial product matches the part of the area model that shows ___.
My product is reasonable because my estimate was ___.
I found the mistake: ___ should be ___ because ___.
d: Multiply with fluency a three-digit number by a two-digit number using the standard algorithm.

mis.m: Writes a quotient digit too small, leaving a remainder larger than the divisor (for example 84 left over when dividing by 32).
mis.why: Students under-estimate each partial quotient and do not check the remainder against the divisor.
mis.fix: Have students circle the remainder at each step and ask, 'Is this less than the divisor?' before moving on.

mis.m: Forgets a zero in the quotient, such as 6,240 ÷ 12 = 52 instead of 520.
mis.why: When a bring-down step does not allow a division, students skip writing 0 in the quotient.
mis.fix: Use a place value chart above the quotient so every place gets a digit, even zero.

mis.m: Rounds 23 to 20 to estimate, then uses that estimate as the exact quotient digit without checking the product.
mis.why: Students treat estimation of quotient digits as the final answer instead of a first try.
mis.fix: Model 'estimate, multiply, compare' explicitly and allow students to adjust a quotient digit up or down.

cra.c: Students share base-ten blocks equally among groups for a smaller example such as 156 ÷ 12, trading flats for rods as needed.
cra.r: Students use an area model with the divisor as the known side, building partial quotients (such as 100, 50, 8) until the area is used up.
cra.a: Students use partial quotients and the standard algorithm side by side, then check with multiplication: quotient × divisor + remainder = dividend.
cra.look: Students record partial quotients in an area model, compare remainders to the divisor, and check every quotient with multiplication.

assess: How did you choose your first partial quotient?
How does your area model match the standard algorithm steps?
advance: What would happen to the quotient if the divisor doubled?
Write a four-digit dividend that divides by 24 with no remainder.

assess: Show me how you checked your answer.
Why is there a zero in the tens place of your quotient?
advance: Can you use a bigger partial quotient to save steps?
How does your remainder fit the story problem?

assess: How many 12s are in 120?
Is your remainder less than 12?
advance: Use your list of multiples of 12 to pick the next partial quotient.
Multiply your answer by 12. Do you get back to the dividend?
support: Provide a list of the divisor's multiples (×1 through ×10) before students start.
Start with partial quotients using friendly chunks like 10 and 100 before the standard algorithm.

stems: I estimated that ___ goes into ___ about ___ times.
My remainder is ___, which is less than ___.
I checked by multiplying ___ × ___ and adding ___.
There is a zero in the quotient because ___.
In this problem, the remainder means ___.
d: Solve with proficiency for quotients of up to a four-digit by two-digit divisor using strategies and the standard algorithm.

mis.m: Represents 0.3 × 0.4 by shading 3 columns and 4 more columns, getting 0.7.
mis.why: Students combine the factors instead of showing the overlap.
mis.fix: Shade 3 tenths one direction and 4 tenths the other direction in different colors and count only the double-shaded squares.

mis.m: Shades the product 0.12 as 12 tenths in the model.
mis.why: Students lose track of the unit: each small square in a hundredths grid is one hundredth.
mis.fix: Have students label one small square '0.01' on the grid before counting the overlap.

mis.m: Expects every product to be greater than both factors, so rejects a model showing 0.5 × 0.6 = 0.30.
mis.why: Whole-number experience suggests multiplying always makes larger amounts.
mis.fix: Ask, 'What is half of 6 tenths?' and let students see on the model that the product is part of a part.

cra.c: Students use base-ten blocks (flat as one whole) or decimal squares to build 2 × 0.35 as two groups of 3 rods and 5 units, then combine.
cra.r: Students draw area models on hundredths grids, shading one factor horizontally and the other vertically, and label the overlap as the product.
cra.a: Students write the equation that matches each model, such as 0.4 × 0.7 = 0.28, and connect it to 4 × 7 = 28.
cra.look: Students shade grids in two colors, count the overlapping hundredths, and write the matching equation.

assess: Which part of your model shows the product?
How do you know each small square is one hundredth?
advance: How would the model change for 1.2 × 0.4?
Why is 0.5 × 0.8 less than 0.8?

assess: Show me 0.6 on your grid.
Count the double-shaded squares. What decimal is that?
advance: Write an equation for your model.
How is this model like the area model for 6 × 3?

assess: How many tenths did you shade going across?
Point to the squares that are shaded twice.
advance: What is the value of one small square?
Say the product as 'hundredths.'
support: Provide pre-printed hundredths grids with the tenths lines darkened.
Use transparent colored overlays so the overlap stands out.

stems: I shaded ___ tenths across and ___ tenths down.
The overlap is ___ hundredths, so the product is ___.
This model shows ___ groups of ___.
The product is less than ___ because ___.
My model matches the equation ___ because ___.
d: Represent multiplication of decimals with products to the hundredths using objects and pictorial models, including area models.

mis.m: Lines up decimal points in the product as in addition, so 2.5 × 1.3 gives 32.5.
mis.why: Students apply the addition rule for aligning decimals to multiplication.
mis.fix: Have students estimate first (about 3 × 1 = 3) and use the estimate to place the decimal point.

mis.m: Counts decimal places incorrectly, such as 0.4 × 0.5 = 2.0 or 0.2.
mis.why: Students drop the zero from 20 hundredths or count places without understanding the product's unit.
mis.fix: Connect to 4 tenths × 5 tenths = 20 hundredths, then write 0.20 and discuss why it equals 0.2.

mis.m: For $3.25 × 4 writes $1,300 or $13.0 and reads it as thirteen hundred dollars.
mis.why: Students multiply whole numbers and lose the money context and the cents place.
mis.fix: Model with coins and bills: 4 groups of $3.25, then compare the total to the computed product.

cra.c: Students use coins and bills or base-ten blocks to show products such as 3 × $1.45, counting dollars, dimes and pennies.
cra.r: Students draw area models with partial products (such as 2 × 1.3 and 0.5 × 1.3) and use number lines to show repeated groups of a decimal.
cra.a: Students multiply as whole numbers, then use place value reasoning or an estimate to place the decimal point, and record equations using properties such as the distributive property.
cra.look: Students estimate before computing, record partial products, and explain decimal placement with place value instead of a memorized trick.

assess: How did you decide where the decimal point goes?
How does 25 × 13 help you find 2.5 × 1.3?
advance: What happens to the product when one factor is ten times smaller?
Create a money problem whose product is $12.60.

assess: What was your estimate before you multiplied?
Show me the partial products in your area model.
advance: Why is 0.4 × 0.5 written as 0.20 or 0.2?
Could you use the distributive property to make this easier?

assess: What is 4 × 5?
How many dollars is 4 groups of $1?
advance: Now think 4 tenths times 5 tenths. Is the answer tenths or hundredths?
Count the coins. Does your product match?
support: Provide play money for money problems so students can count the total.
Give a place value chart to record whole-number products and then shift digits.

stems: I estimated ___ × ___, so my product should be about ___.
___ tenths times ___ tenths equals ___ hundredths.
I used the whole-number product ___ to help me find ___.
The decimal point goes ___ because ___.
In this money problem, the total cost is ___ because ___.
d: Solve for products of decimals to the hundredths, including situations involving money, using strategies based on place-value understandings, properties of operations, and the relationship to the multiplication of whole numbers.

mis.m: Models 4.8 ÷ 4 by making 4 groups but splits only the wholes, leaving the 8 tenths out.
mis.why: Students focus on the whole-number part and ignore decimal pieces.
mis.fix: Have students build all of 4.8 with base-ten blocks and check that no pieces are left on the table when the groups are complete.

mis.m: Does not regroup a leftover whole into tenths, so gets stuck on 3.6 ÷ 2 with one flat left over.
mis.why: Students do not see that one whole can be traded for 10 tenths.
mis.fix: Model trading one flat for 10 rods and ask, 'Now can we share them equally?'

mis.m: In an area model, labels the missing side with the dividend rather than the quotient.
mis.why: Students mix up which dimension is known and which is unknown.
mis.fix: Label the area and the known side first, then mark the unknown side with a question mark before solving.

cra.c: Students share base-ten blocks or place value disks equally among groups, regrouping ones into tenths and tenths into hundredths as needed.
cra.r: Students draw area models with the divisor as one side and the dividend as the area, or strip diagrams split into equal parts, labeling each section's decimal value.
cra.a: Students write the division equation that matches the model, such as 7.25 ÷ 5 = 1.45, and check with multiplication.
cra.look: Students trade blocks to keep sharing, and label area model sections with decimal partial quotients.

assess: Why did you trade that one for ten tenths?
How does your area model show the quotient?
advance: How would the model change if the divisor were 10?
Which other division problem has the same model, and why?

assess: Show me how you shared the tenths.
What is in each group?
advance: Write the equation that matches your model.
Check: does your quotient times the divisor equal the dividend?

assess: How many groups are you making?
How many wholes go in each group?
advance: You have one whole left. What can you trade it for?
Now share the tenths. How many does each group get?
support: Provide a sharing mat with circles drawn for each group.
Start with dividends that need no regrouping, such as 6.9 ÷ 3.

stems: I shared ___ into ___ equal groups.
I traded one ___ for ten ___ so I could keep sharing.
Each group has ___, so the quotient is ___.
In my area model, the side I found is ___.
I checked my quotient by multiplying ___ × ___.
d: Represent quotients of decimals to the hundredths, up to four-digit dividends and two-digit whole number divisors, using objects and pictorial models, including area models.

mis.m: Forgets to place the decimal point in the quotient above the decimal point in the dividend, so 25.5 ÷ 5 becomes 51.
mis.why: Students compute as whole numbers and do not track place value.
mis.fix: Have students place the decimal point in the quotient before they start dividing, and check with an estimate.

mis.m: Stops dividing when a remainder appears, writing 9.3 ÷ 6 = 1 R 3.3 instead of continuing.
mis.why: Whole-number division ended with a remainder, so students do not annex zeros to continue.
mis.fix: Show that 3.3 = 3.30 and model continuing the division into the hundredths place.

mis.m: Misses a zero in the quotient, such as 8.24 ÷ 8 = 1.3 instead of 1.03.
mis.why: When the tenths digit cannot be divided, students skip it.
mis.fix: Use a place value chart over the quotient and ask, 'How many groups of 8 are in 2 tenths?' so they write 0.

cra.c: Students share money (bills, dimes and pennies) for problems such as $12.48 ÷ 4 to make sense of each quotient digit.
cra.r: Students use area models with partial quotients in ones, tenths and hundredths, and strip diagrams to show equal groups.
cra.a: Students use the standard algorithm with the decimal point placed first, then check by multiplying the quotient by the divisor.
cra.look: Students estimate first, place the decimal point before dividing, and check quotients with multiplication.

assess: Why does the decimal point go there in your quotient?
How did your estimate help you?
advance: What would change if the dividend were ten times greater?
Write a problem where the quotient has a zero in the tenths place.

assess: Show me the partial quotients in your area model.
How did you handle the leftover tenths?
advance: Check your answer with multiplication.
Does your quotient make sense in the money problem?

assess: About how much is $12 ÷ 4?
Where does the decimal point go before you start?
advance: How many groups of 4 are in 4 tenths?
Can you write a zero and keep dividing?
support: Provide graph paper with a vertical line marking the decimal point column.
Use money manipulatives for each problem until place value placement is consistent.

stems: My estimate is ___, so my quotient should be about ___.
I placed the decimal point in the quotient ___ because ___.
I wrote a zero in the ___ place because ___.
I checked by multiplying ___ × ___ = ___.
In this problem, each person gets ___ because ___.
d: Solve for quotients of decimals to the hundredths, up to four-digit dividends and two-digit whole number divisions, using strategies and algorithms, including the standard algorithm.

mis.m: Adds numerators and denominators: one-half plus one-third equals two-fifths.
mis.why: Students apply whole-number addition to each part of the fraction without thinking about the size of the pieces.
mis.fix: Have students show both fractions with fraction strips and ask, 'Can two-fifths be right if it is less than one-half?'

mis.m: Finds a common denominator but does not change the numerator, writing 1/2 as 1/6.
mis.why: Students change the denominator alone, not seeing that both parts must be multiplied by the same factor.
mis.fix: Use an area model to cut each part into the same number of smaller pieces and count the new numerator.

mis.m: Uses fraction models whose wholes are different sizes, then compares or combines unequal pieces.
mis.why: Students do not notice the whole must stay the same for fractions to be combined.
mis.fix: Line up fraction strips under one whole strip before adding, and ask, 'Do both fractions refer to the same whole?'

cra.c: Students use fraction strips or fraction tiles under the same whole to find pieces that fit both fractions, then trade for equal-sized pieces.
cra.r: Students draw area models or number lines partitioned into a common unit, and strip diagrams for word problems, labeling each part.
cra.a: Students write equivalent fractions with a common denominator, add or subtract, and use properties of operations such as regrouping to combine whole numbers and fractions.
cra.look: Students line up strips under the same whole, rename fractions with equal-sized pieces, and explain why the denominator stays the same in the sum.

assess: How did you find pieces that work for both fractions?
Why does the denominator stay the same when you add?
advance: Is there more than one common denominator you could use? Which is easier?
Write a subtraction problem with a difference of five-twelfths.

assess: Show me both fractions on the same whole.
What size pieces did you trade for?
advance: How can you check your answer with a benchmark like one-half?
Can you rearrange the parts to add the whole numbers first?

assess: Which strip is longer, one-half or one-third?
Are these pieces the same size?
advance: Find a strip that fits exactly under both one-half and one-third.
How many sixths make one-half?
support: Provide a fraction wall with all strips aligned to the same whole.
Start with denominators where one is a multiple of the other, such as halves and fourths.

stems: I renamed ___ as ___ so the pieces are the same size.
The common unit is ___ because ___.
___ plus ___ equals ___ because ___.
My answer is reasonable because it is close to the benchmark ___.
I disagree with adding the denominators because ___.
d: Represent and solve addition and subtraction of fractions with unequal denominators referring to the same whole using objects and pictorial models and properties of operations.

mis.m: Multiplies both the numerator and denominator by the whole number: 3 × two-fifths becomes six-fifteenths.
mis.why: Students think multiplying a fraction means multiplying both parts, not counting more pieces of the same size.
mis.fix: Show 3 groups of two-fifths with fraction strips and count the fifths: 6 fifths.

mis.m: Thinks 4 × three-fourths must be less than three-fourths, or that one-third × 12 must be greater than 12.
mis.why: Students hold one fixed belief about multiplication and do not reason about the size of the factors.
mis.fix: Ask students to predict the size of the product using a benchmark before they compute, then check with a model.

mis.m: Draws an area model with unequal parts or with parts that refer to different wholes.
mis.why: Students sketch quickly and lose the meaning of equal parts of the same whole.
mis.fix: Have students fold paper strips or use a grid so each part is equal, and label the whole before shading.

cra.c: Students build groups of fractions with fraction tiles (4 groups of two-thirds) and find a fraction of a set with counters (one-third of 12).
cra.r: Students draw area models and strip diagrams split into equal parts, and use number lines to show repeated jumps of a fraction.
cra.a: Students write equations such as 4 × 2/3 = 8/3 = 2 2/3 and connect each to its model.
cra.look: Students build or draw equal groups of fractional parts, label the whole, and match the model to an equation.

assess: How does your model show 4 groups of two-thirds?
Why is the product greater than one?
advance: How would the product change if the fraction were two-sixths?
Write a story problem for one-fourth × 20.

assess: Show me one group on your strip diagram.
How many thirds did you count in all?
advance: Write the product as a mixed number.
Is the product more or less than the whole number? Why?

assess: How many groups are there?
How big is each piece?
advance: Count the pieces in all the groups. How many thirds?
How many thirds make a whole?
support: Provide fraction tiles and a mat with circles drawn for each group.
Start with unit fractions, such as 5 × one-fourth, before non-unit fractions.

stems: I made ___ groups of ___.
In all, there are ___ pieces that are each ___ of the whole.
The product is ___, which is the same as ___ wholes and ___.
The product is less than ___ because I am finding part of it.
My model matches my equation because ___.
d: Represent and solve multiplication of a whole number and a fraction that refers to the same whole using objects and pictorial models, including area models.

mis.m: Thinks 7 ÷ 1/3 equals 7/3 or 2 1/3, dividing 7 into 3 parts.
mis.why: Students read 'divided by one-third' as 'divided by 3.'
mis.fix: Ask, 'How many thirds fit in 7 wholes?' and have students count the thirds on a number line or with fraction strips.

mis.m: Thinks one-third ÷ 7 must be greater than one-third because division with fractions 'makes bigger.'
mis.why: Students overgeneralize from whole number ÷ unit fraction problems.
mis.fix: Have students split a one-third strip into 7 equal parts and compare one part to the whole strip.

mis.m: Draws an area model for one-third ÷ 7 but labels each small part as one-seventh.
mis.why: Students name the part by the divisor instead of relating it to the original whole.
mis.fix: Extend the 7 cuts across the whole rectangle so students count 21 equal parts and name one as one twenty-first.

cra.c: Students use fraction strips or paper folding: cut one-third into 7 equal parts, and count how many one-third strips fit in 7 whole strips.
cra.r: Students draw area models and number lines, partitioning the whole to show both 'share into groups' and 'how many groups' meanings.
cra.a: Students write the matching equations, such as 1/3 ÷ 7 = 1/21 and 7 ÷ 1/3 = 21, and check each with multiplication.
cra.look: Students fold or cut strips and say either 'how many thirds fit' or 'one-third shared into 7 parts,' pointing to their model.

assess: What question does 7 ÷ one-third ask?
How does your area model show one-third ÷ 7?
advance: Why are the quotients of these two problems so different?
Write a story for each problem.

assess: Show me how many thirds are in one whole.
Into how many parts did you cut the one-third?
advance: How can you check your answer with multiplication?
What fraction of the whole is one small piece?

assess: How many thirds make 1 whole?
Point to one-third on the strip.
advance: Then how many thirds make 2 wholes? 7 wholes?
If you cut this third into 7 parts, how many of those parts fill the whole?
support: Provide pre-cut fraction strips in thirds and fourths for hands-on counting.
Use a number line marked in thirds so students can count jumps.

stems: Seven divided by one-third asks how many ___ fit in ___.
When I share one-third into ___ equal parts, each part is ___ of the whole.
The quotient is greater than ___ because ___.
I checked by multiplying ___ × ___.
My model shows ___ because ___.
d: Represent division of a unit fraction by a whole number and the division of a whole n umber by a unit fraction such as 1/3 ÷ 7 and 7 ÷ 1/3 using objects and pictorial models, including area models.

mis.m: Lines up the last digits instead of the decimal points: 4.5 + 2.36 = 2.81.
mis.why: Students right-justify numbers as they do with whole numbers.
mis.fix: Have students write each number on a place value chart and annex zeros so all numbers have the same number of places.

mis.m: When subtracting 6 − 2.47, writes 4.47 or brings down the 47.
mis.why: Students do not see that 6 is 6.00 and needs regrouping.
mis.fix: Write 6 as 6.00 and model regrouping with place value disks or money.

mis.m: For 3 1/4 − 1 3/4 subtracts the smaller fraction from the larger, getting 2 2/4.
mis.why: Students subtract fractional parts in whichever order avoids regrouping.
mis.fix: Rename 3 1/4 as 2 5/4 using fraction strips, then subtract.

cra.c: Students use place value disks or money for decimal sums and differences, and fraction strips for regrouping mixed numbers.
cra.r: Students use number lines and strip diagrams to show jumps or compare parts, labeling decimal and fraction values.
cra.a: Students compute with standard algorithms for decimals and with common denominators for fractions, and use estimates and benchmarks to check reasonableness.
cra.look: Students align decimal points, annex zeros, rename mixed numbers, and check answers against an estimate.

assess: Why did you write 6 as 6.00?
How did you rename the mixed number?
advance: Which strategy is most efficient for this problem, and why?
Find two different decimals with a sum of 10.

assess: Show me how you lined up the numbers.
What is your estimate?
advance: Does your answer make sense compared to your estimate?
Could you add on instead of subtracting?

assess: Where is the decimal point in each number?
How many fourths are in one whole?
advance: Write a zero so both numbers have the same places.
Trade one whole for four fourths. What do you have now?
support: Provide graph paper with a decimal point column marked.
Give fraction strips for renaming mixed numbers.

stems: I lined up the decimal points because ___.
I wrote ___ as ___ so I could subtract.
I renamed ___ as ___ because ___.
My estimate was ___, and my answer is ___.
I added on from ___ to ___ to find the difference.
d: Add and subtract positive rational numbers fluently.

mis.m: Computes 6 ÷ 1/4 as 1.5 or one-and-a-half by dividing 6 by 4.
mis.why: Students treat the unit fraction as its denominator and divide.
mis.fix: Ask, 'How many fourths are in one whole? In 6 wholes?' and count on a number line.

mis.m: Computes 1/5 ÷ 3 as 3/5 or 15.
mis.why: Students multiply or flip without understanding what the problem asks.
mis.fix: Have students draw one-fifth and split it into 3 equal parts, then name one part of the whole.

mis.m: Uses a memorized procedure with the wrong number inverted, getting 5 ÷ 1/2 = 2/5.
mis.why: Students apply a rule they do not understand and misremember which number to flip.
mis.fix: Return to the meaning 'how many halves in 5?' and have students check every answer with multiplication.

cra.c: Students use fraction tiles to count how many unit fractions fit in a whole number, and fold paper strips to share a unit fraction among groups.
cra.r: Students use number lines marked in unit fractions and area models partitioned both ways to show each quotient.
cra.a: Students write and solve division equations, noticing that whole number ÷ 1/b = whole number × b and 1/b ÷ c = 1/(b × c), and verify with multiplication.
cra.look: Students use number lines or area models to justify quotients and check answers with multiplication.

assess: What pattern do you notice in whole number divided by a unit fraction?
How does your area model show one-fifth divided by 3?
advance: Will the pattern work for 8 ÷ one-sixth? Test it.
Write a story where one-fourth is shared among 3 people.

assess: How many halves are in 1? In 5?
What is one part called after you split the fifth?
advance: Check your answer: does quotient × divisor equal the dividend?
Is the quotient greater or less than the dividend? Why?

assess: How many fourths are in one whole?
Show me one-fifth on your strip.
advance: Count the fourths in 2 wholes, then in 6 wholes.
Split that fifth into 3 parts. How many of those parts fit in the whole?
support: Provide number lines pre-marked in unit fractions.
Use real objects such as a sheet of paper or a sandwich to act out sharing a unit fraction.

stems: There are ___ one-fourths in ___ wholes.
When one-fifth is split into ___ parts, each part is ___.
The quotient is greater than the dividend because ___.
I checked my answer by multiplying ___ × ___.
I noticed a pattern: ___.
d: Divide whole numbers by unit fractions and unit fractions by whole numbers.

mis.m: Says 1 is prime because it can only be divided by 1 and itself.
mis.why: Students memorize 'divisible by 1 and itself' without noting that a prime has exactly two factors.
mis.fix: Have students list factors of 1, 2, 3 and 4 and count them, then define prime as exactly two factors.

mis.m: Calls all odd numbers prime, so labels 9, 15 or 21 as prime.
mis.why: Students notice 2 is the only even prime and overgeneralize that odd means prime.
mis.fix: Have students build rectangular arrays with counters for 9 and 15 to find more than one array.

mis.m: Says 2 is composite because it is even.
mis.why: Students connect 'even' with 'composite' because most even numbers are composite.
mis.fix: Build arrays for 2: only 1 × 2 works, so it has exactly two factors.

cra.c: Students build all possible rectangular arrays with square tiles or counters for numbers 1 to 30; numbers with only one array (1 row) are prime.
cra.r: Students draw arrays on grid paper and record factor pairs in a T-chart, and shade primes on a hundreds chart.
cra.a: Students list factor pairs and classify each number as prime (exactly two factors) or composite (more than two factors), explaining why 1 is neither.
cra.look: Students build or sketch arrays, list factor pairs systematically, and justify classifications by counting factors.

assess: How do you know you found all the factor pairs?
Why is 1 neither prime nor composite?
advance: Is every odd number prime? Prove it with an example.
Find two prime numbers whose sum is 30.

assess: Show me the arrays you made for 12.
How many factors does 13 have?
advance: What do all the arrays for prime numbers have in common?
Can a composite number have an odd number of factors? Try 16.

assess: Can you make a rectangle with 7 tiles in more than one way?
Is 6 divisible by 2?
advance: List the factors of 6 in pairs.
How many factors does 7 have? So is it prime or composite?
support: Provide a multiplication chart to check factor pairs.
Start with numbers to 20 and square tiles before moving to larger numbers.

stems: The factors of ___ are ___.
___ is prime because it has exactly two factors: ___ and ___.
___ is composite because ___.
One is neither prime nor composite because ___.
I disagree that all odd numbers are prime because ___.
d: Identify prime and composite numbers.

mis.m: Writes one equation for only the first step and calls that the answer.
mis.why: Students stop after one operation instead of reading the full question.
mis.fix: Have students underline the question and draw a strip diagram for the whole problem before writing any equation.

mis.m: Uses the letter for something other than the unknown, or uses the same letter for two different unknowns.
mis.why: Students do not define what the letter stands for.
mis.fix: Require a 'Let n = ...' statement in words before writing the equation.

mis.m: Chooses the operation by key words, such as adding whenever 'in all' appears even when the problem needs multiplication.
mis.why: Key-word strategies replace understanding of the situation.
mis.fix: Have students act out or draw the situation first and ask, 'Are these equal groups or different amounts?'

cra.c: Students act out the situation with counters, base-ten blocks or play money to understand each step.
cra.r: Students draw strip diagrams showing all the parts and the unknown, labeling the unknown with a letter.
cra.a: Students write one or more equations with a letter for the unknown, such as (4 × 12) + 15 = p, solve them, and check the answer in the context.
cra.look: Students draw strip diagrams, define the letter in words, and check that the solution answers the question asked.

assess: What does your letter stand for?
How does your strip diagram match your equation?
advance: Can you write the whole problem as one equation?
Change one number in the problem. Which part of your equation changes?

assess: What is the first thing you need to find?
Show me the unknown in your strip diagram.
advance: Does your answer make sense in the story?
Could you solve it in a different order?

assess: What is the question asking?
Are these equal groups?
advance: Draw a box for each group. How many in each?
What letter will you use for the part we do not know?
support: Provide a strip diagram template with labeled parts.
Break the problem into one step at a time with a guiding question for each.

stems: The letter ___ stands for ___.
First I need to find ___, then ___.
My equation is ___ because ___.
My answer makes sense because ___.
My strip diagram shows ___.
d: Represent and solve multi-step problems involving the four operations with whole numbers using equations with a letter standing for the unknown quantity.

mis.m: For y = 3x writes the pattern 3, 6, 9 but pairs them with x-values 0, 1, 2, shifting the table.
mis.why: Students generate a list of multiples without applying the rule to each x.
mis.fix: Have students write the substitution for each row, such as y = 3 × 2, before recording y.

mis.m: Plots (2, 6) as 6 across and 2 up.
mis.why: Students reverse the order of the ordered pair.
mis.fix: Teach 'walk across the x-axis, then climb up the y-axis' and have students trace with a finger.

mis.m: Confuses y = x + a with y = ax, writing 5, 10, 15 for y = x + 5.
mis.why: Students see the number 5 and default to multiples.
mis.fix: Have students read the rule aloud as 'add 5 to x' or 'multiply x by 5' and test one row before completing the table.

cra.c: Students build each term with counters or connecting cubes (for example 3 cubes per stack) and line up stacks to see the pattern grow.
cra.r: Students complete input-output tables and plot the ordered pairs on a coordinate grid.
cra.a: Students write the rule as y = ax or y = x + a, generate values for given x, and describe how the graph shows the rule.
cra.look: Students fill tables by applying the rule to each input, then plot points on a coordinate grid and describe the pattern.

assess: How did you use the rule to find this y-value?
What does the point (4, 12) mean in this pattern?
advance: Without plotting, will (10, 30) be on this graph? How do you know?
How would the graph look different for y = x + 3?

assess: Show me how you plotted (2, 6).
What do you notice about the points on your graph?
advance: Find the y-value when x is 8.
Write the rule in words.

assess: What is 3 × 1?
Which number in the pair do you go across first?
advance: Now use the rule for x = 2.
Put your finger at 0, move across 2, then up 6.
support: Provide a partially completed table and a coordinate grid with labeled axes.
Use colored pencils for the x column and the x-axis to connect them.

stems: The rule is ___, so when x is ___, y is ___.
The ordered pair ___ means ___.
I plotted the point by moving ___ across and ___ up.
The points on the graph ___.
This rule is additive or multiplicative because ___.
d: Generate a numerical pattern when given a rule in the form y = ax or y = x + a and graph.

mis.m: Calls y = 2x additive because the y-values go up by 2 each time.
mis.why: Students look only at the change in y down the column instead of comparing x and y across a row.
mis.fix: Have students describe the relationship across each row ('What do I do to x to get y?') as well as down the column.

mis.m: Assumes all straight-line graphs are the same kind of pattern.
mis.why: Both additive and multiplicative patterns in this grade appear as straight lines, so students do not look further.
mis.fix: Have students check whether the graph goes through (0, 0); multiplicative patterns of the form y = ax do, additive ones with a > 0 do not.

mis.m: Labels a table as multiplicative after testing only one row, such as (2, 4) where both 2 + 2 and 2 × 2 work.
mis.why: Students stop after one row that fits a rule.
mis.fix: Require students to test the rule on at least three rows before naming the pattern.

cra.c: Students build two patterns side by side with connecting cubes: one adds 3 each time from a starting stack, one is 3 times the step number.
cra.r: Students compare tables and graph both patterns on the same coordinate grid, noting where each line starts.
cra.a: Students write rules such as y = x + 3 and y = 3x and explain in words how each table and graph shows the relationship.
cra.look: Students test rules on several rows, compare graphs on one grid, and explain the difference in their own words.

assess: What do you do to each x-value to get the y-value?
How does the graph show whether this pattern is additive?
advance: Make a table that is additive and one that is multiplicative with the same y-value when x is 1.
Where would the two lines cross?

assess: Test your rule on the third row.
Where does your line start on the graph?
advance: Why does a multiplicative graph go through (0, 0)?
Write the rule for this table.

assess: Look at the first row. What happened to 1 to make 4?
Does adding 3 work for the next row too?
advance: Try multiplying. Does that work for every row?
Point to where the line starts on the y-axis.
support: Provide tables with an extra column for 'what I did to x.'
Use only one-operation rules with small numbers first.

stems: The pattern is additive because ___.
The pattern is multiplicative because each y-value is ___ times the x-value.
I tested the rule on ___ rows.
On the graph, the line starts at ___, so ___.
The difference between these two patterns is ___.
d: Recognize the difference between additive and multiplicative numerical patterns given in a table or graph.

mis.m: Ignores parentheses and works left to right: 3 + (4 × 2) and (3 + 4) × 2 both get 14.
mis.why: Students see parentheses as decoration rather than as a grouping symbol.
mis.fix: Have students evaluate the same numbers with and without grouping and compare the results side by side.

mis.m: Thinks brackets mean multiplication or a different operation.
mis.why: Brackets are new at this grade and students do not recognize them as another grouping symbol.
mis.fix: Introduce brackets as 'parentheses around parentheses' and color-code each level of grouping.

mis.m: In 2 × [5 + (6 − 1)] evaluates the brackets first and skips the inner parentheses.
mis.why: Students treat the outer symbol as the first step instead of working from the innermost group.
mis.fix: Have students circle the innermost grouping symbol first and evaluate outward.

cra.c: Students use counters in cups or bags to show grouped quantities, such as one bag of (4 + 2) counters, then 3 bags.
cra.r: Students draw strip diagrams or boxes around grouped parts to show what is evaluated together.
cra.a: Students describe in words what each expression means, such as '3 times the sum of 4 and 2,' and match words to expressions with parentheses and brackets.
cra.look: Students circle grouping symbols, describe expressions in words, and compare values with different groupings.

assess: What do the parentheses tell you to do first?
How are the brackets different from the parentheses here?
advance: Where could you add parentheses to 8 + 4 × 2 to make 24?
Write an expression in words and then with brackets.

assess: Read this expression in words.
Which part did you work first?
advance: Does moving the parentheses change the value? Show me.
Match this expression to a story.

assess: Point to the parentheses.
What is 4 + 2?
advance: Now what do you do with that answer?
Circle the innermost group first.
support: Provide expression cards with grouping symbols color-coded.
Start with only parentheses before adding brackets.

stems: The parentheses mean ___.
I worked ___ first because it is inside the ___.
In words, this expression means ___.
Moving the parentheses changed the value because ___.
The brackets group ___.
d: Describe the meaning of parentheses and brackets in a numeric expression.
